finding: The live range of $1,075-$3,700 starts too low and tops out a little low for trucks. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2016 Honda Civic 1.5L turbo about $1,412-$3,410 (11.5-18.8 hr); midsize 2018 Honda Accord 1.5L turbo about $1,413-$3,128 (11.5-17.0 hr); truck 2012 F-150 5.0L, both heads, about $2,842-$4,349 (20.9-24.2 hr); luxury 2016 Cadillac Escalade 6.2L, both heads, about $1,358-$2,157 (9.9-11.1 hr). The lowest totals we can build are about $1,360-$1,410, and they pair a manufacturer warranty time with the cheapest parts found (on the two Hondas the head gasket alone at about $32; on the Escalade a gasket-and-bolt set without the intake, exhaust and valve cover gaskets), with no machine-shop work, coolant, oil or air-conditioning service, so real quotes start higher; nothing supports $1,075. At the top, both heads on a full-size truck with overhead cams come to about $4,350, above $3,700. A range of roughly $1,400-$4,400 fits the evidence better. RepairPal ($2,572-$3,386 national; F-150 $3,474-$4,603) and CarParts.com ($2,400-$3,200) sit inside our built totals; only a 2023 J.D. Power article ($1,000-$3,000) supports the live low end. How solid the labor times are: three of the four low ends are now manufacturer warranty times for the example vehicle itself. Economy: the example was changed from a 2015 Toyota Corolla to a 2016 Honda Civic 1.5L turbo because Honda prints the time and Toyota does not; Honda's warranty flat-rate time for that car is 11.5 hr (11.9 hr with a new cylinder head). Midsize: the example was changed from a 2016 Toyota Camry to a 2018 Honda Accord 1.5L turbo for the same reason; Honda states 11.5 hr for both the CVT and the manual car (12.0 hr with a new head), and its other 2026 head gasket bulletins give 10.8-12.4 hr. The economy and midsize high ends are weak and are not Honda figures: 18.8 hr is a technician forum post quoting a labor guide for a Toyota Prius 1.8L, and 17 hr is a parts retailer's statement about Toyota Camrys with no model years given. They are kept as the only stated labor-guide times found for small and midsize four-cylinder cars, because a warranty time alone understates what shops bill; no second stated time for the Civic or Accord themselves was found. The truck times are Ford warranty times for replacing both cylinder heads on an F-150 with the 2.7L V6 (20.9-24.2 hr), not the 5.0L V8; a technician forum post puts the 5.0L book time at about 24 hours, which agrees. The truck example was not moved to the 2.7L because no priced aftermarket head gasket set for that engine was found. Luxury: the Escalade low end (9.9 hr, both heads) is GM's own warranty time for that vehicle; the high end (11.1 hr) is an Acura warranty time for a 2025-26 ADX four-cylinder, a comparable luxury-brand vehicle and not the example. Both are warranty times, so the luxury total is a floor, and it should not be read as the price for a European luxury car: no stated time was found for one (BMW bulletins point to BMW's own labor-time system), and overhead-cam turbo engines generally take longer than this pushrod V8 (GM allows 14.3 hr for the same engine in a Corvette). Parts caveats: on the Civic and Accord the low figure is an aftermarket head gasket alone and the high figure is Honda's full head gasket kit at list, so the low end leaves out the other gaskets the job uses; head bolts were not priced for either Honda; the truck bolt-set listing does not say whether it covers both heads; the luxury high parts figure prices 19 of the 20 head bolts; fluids were not priced.
extras: Machine-shop work is the biggest add-on: the head is normally checked for flatness and cracks and resurfaced, and a warped or cracked head means more machining or a replacement head. Quotes also commonly add coolant, engine oil and filter, thermostat, spark plugs, a diagnosis fee (cooling-system pressure test or combustion-gas test), shop supplies and sales tax. Many shops recommend doing the timing chain or belt, water pump and related seals while the engine is apart, and V engines may be quoted for one head or both, so check which the quote covers.
